Mimic

/MIM-ik/ - rhymes with gimmick · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Mimic means to imitate closely in sound, appearance, or behavior.

The impressionist could mimic the principal's slow, careful 'outstanding' so exactly that students spun around expecting detention.

Worked Example

Engineers built the rescue robot to mimic a cockroach: the same six-legged scuttle, the same trick of flattening its body to slip through cracks in rubble. The imitation is strictly practical—what survives a collapsing building for the insect survives it for the machine.

Mimic is closer than 'copy': copying can be loose and one-time, while mimicking reproduces the look, sound, or behavior of the original closely—often live and in motion.

How Mimic Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

imitate

imitate: the general word for following a model

impersonate

impersonate: to imitate a specific person so as to pass as them

parrot

parrot: to repeat words mechanically, with no understanding

Antonyms

invent

invent: to produce something genuinely new rather than copy it

improvise

improvise: to make something up on the spot, following no model

How Strong Is It? — echo → mimic → impersonate

echo vs. mimic

echo vs. mimic: An echo repeats without shaping—sound bounced straight back; to mimic is to study the original and reproduce its manner deliberately.

impersonate vs. mimic

impersonate vs. mimic: Impersonate goes beyond mimic: the mimic reproduces a voice or a walk for a moment, while the impersonator sustains the whole identity, trying to pass as the person.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mim

Root — mim: imitator, actor (from Greek mimos)

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: relating to, like

Put it together

Put it together: Mim (imitator) + -ic (like) = like an imitator. Greek mimos was the actor-imitator of the ancient stage, and his family spread through English: mime, mimicry, pantomime. Mimic keeps the stage sense alive—to mimic is to perform someone else's manner, not merely to resemble it.

Use the root in a new word: mime

Use the root in a new word: mime: The street mime acted out an entire thunderstorm—wind, umbrella, puddle—without one word.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Mimic is neutral about motive: lyrebirds, robots, and comedians all mimic, skillfully and often harmlessly. Travesty, later in this unit, is what an imitation becomes when it degrades the original. Use mimic for close, faithful imitation of sound, look, or behavior; use impersonate when someone tries to pass as a specific person.
